## Today {.scrollable}

Two new families of continuous random variables:

- **Normal:** the famous bell curve. It can take values anywhere on the real line;
- **Gamma:** a flexible family for positive quantities (eg. waiting times) that generalizes the exponential distribution.

Today we just enumerate basic facts. Derivations come later. We also continue to practice that basic skill:

> event in words $\to$ probability statement $\to$ formula involving CDF $\to$ `R` commands

# Part 1: The normal distribution

## Meet the bell curve {.scrollable}

A random variable $X$ has a **normal** (or **Gaussian**) distribution if its PDF is

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}\right),\qquad -\infty<x<\infty.
$$

We write $X\sim\text{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$, where $\sigma>0$.

- $E(X)=\mu$: the center and axis of symmetry.
- $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$: the variance; $\sigma$ is the **standard deviation**.
- The total area under the curve is 1.

```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 600)
plot(x, dnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue4",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Density", main = "The standard bell curve")
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
```

## Normal PDF = constant $\times$ kernel {.scrollable}

As with **every PMF or PDF**, separate the formula into two pieces:

$$
f(x)=\underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}}_{\text{normalizing constant}}
\;\times\;
\underbrace{\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)}_{\text{kernel}}.
$$

- The **kernel** determines the shape as a function of $x$;
- The **normalizing constant** rescales that shape so the total area is **1**;
- For fixed $\mu$ and $\sigma$, the constant does **not** depend on $x$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
mu <- 0; sd <- 1.5
x <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 700)
kernel <- exp(-(x - mu)^2 / (2 * sd^2))
plot(x, kernel, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#D55E00",
     ylim = c(0, 1.05), xlab = "x", ylab = "Height",
     main = "Same shape; the constant fixes the area")
lines(x, dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sd), lwd = 3, col = "#0072B2")
legend("topright", c("Kernel", "Normalized PDF"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
```

## Free integral identity!

Because PDFs must integrate to 1, the formula for the bell curve implies a free integral identity:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^\infty
\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)
\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}.
$$

It's true *for any* $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\sigma>0$. If you are prepared to recognize this, it can simplify future calculations tremendously!



## What does $\mu$ do? {.scrollable}

You can show that $\mu$ is the location of the peak (the *maximizer*). Changing $\mu$ slides the bell curve horizontally, without changing its shape.

```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(-8, 8, length.out = 600)
plot(x, dnorm(x, -3, 1), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#0072B2",
     ylim = c(0, 0.43), xlab = "x", ylab = "Density",
     main = "Same spread, different centers")
lines(x, dnorm(x, 0, 1), lwd = 3, col = "#D55E00")
lines(x, dnorm(x, 3, 1), lwd = 3, col = "#009E73")
legend("topright", c("mu = -3", "mu = 0", "mu = 3"),
       col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
```

## What does $\sigma$ do? {.scrollable}

You showed on Problem Set 0 that $\sigma$ is the distance between the peak and the *inflection points*:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-concavity
#| fig-asp: 0.5

mu <- 0
sigma <- 1

x <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 1000)
y <- dnorm(x, mu, sigma)

par(mar = c(5, 1, 1, 1))

plot(x, y, type = "n",
     xlim = c(-3.75, 3.75), ylim = c(0, .5),
     axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "",
     ylab = "",
     yaxs = "i")

## Background
rect(-3.75, 0, mu - sigma, .5, col = "#FFF0E6", border = NA)
rect(mu - sigma, 0, mu + sigma, .5, col = "#E5E5FF", border = NA)
rect(mu + sigma, 0, 3.75, .5, col = "#FFF0E6", border = NA)

## Density
lines(x, y, col = "#FF160F", lwd = 3)

## Axes
axis(1,
     at = c(10*min(x), mu - sigma, mu, mu + sigma, 10*max(x)),
     labels = c(NA, expression(mu - sigma),
                expression(mu),
                expression(mu + sigma),
                NA),
     lwd = 1.5)

#axis(1, at = c(mu - sigma, mu + sigma),
#     labels = FALSE, tcl = 0.5, lwd = 1.5)

## Concavity boundaries
abline(v = c(mu - sigma, mu + sigma), lwd = 1.5)

## Dashed line from x-axis to the peak
segments(mu, 0, mu, dnorm(mu, mu, sigma),
         lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)

## Labels
text(-2.75, .47, "concave up", col = "#FD9409", cex = 1.2)
text(mu,    .47, "concave down", col = "blue", cex = 1.2)
text( 2.75, .47, "concave up", col = "#FD9409", cex = 1.2)
```

## What does $\sigma$ do? {.scrollable}

Changing $\sigma$ changes the **spread**. A smaller standard deviation means a narrower, taller bell curve. Changing the spread must simultaneously alter the height because total area 1 must be preserved at all times.

```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(-8, 8, length.out = 600)
plot(x, dnorm(x, 0, 0.6), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#0072B2",
     ylim = c(0, 0.7), xlab = "x", ylab = "Density",
     main = "Same center, different spreads")
lines(x, dnorm(x, 0, 1.2), lwd = 3, col = "#D55E00")
lines(x, dnorm(x, 0, 2.4), lwd = 3, col = "#009E73")
legend("topright", c("sd = 0.6", "sd = 1.2", "sd = 2.4"),
       col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
```

**Watch out:** $\text{N}(10, 4)$ has standard deviation **2**, not 4.

## The 68–95–99.7 rule {.scrollable}

Approximately:

- 68% of the probability lies within **one** standard deviation of the mean;
- 95% lies within **two**;
- 99.7% lies within **three**.

```{r}
#| echo: false
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3.3, 2.5, 2.2, 0.5))
x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 801)
for (k in 1:3) {
  y <- dnorm(x)
  plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = paste0(k, " sd: ", round(100 * (pnorm(k) - pnorm(-k)), 1), "%"),
       ylim = c(0, 0.43), axes = FALSE)
  polygon(c(-k, x[x >= -k & x <= k], k),
          c(0, y[x >= -k & x <= k], 0),
          col = adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.5), border = NA)
  lines(x, y, lwd = 2)
  axis(1, at = c(-k, 0, k))
  box()
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 500

library(shiny)

discrete_pmf <- function(x, p, xlim = c(min(x) - 1, max(x) + 1), label = "", add_mean = FALSE){
  plot(x, p,
       pch = 19,
       cex = 1,
       xlab = "",
       ylab = "",
       main = "",
       ylim = c(0, 1.05 * max(p)),
       yaxs = "i",
       yaxt = "n",
       xlim = xlim,
       xaxt = "n",
       bty = "n"
  )
  segments(x,
           rep(0, length(x) + 1),
           x1 = x,
           y1 = p,
           lwd = 3
  )
  axis(1, at = floor(xlim[1]):ceiling(xlim[2]), cex.axis = 1)
  axis(2, at = seq(0, 1, length.out = 11), las = 1, cex.axis = 1.5)
  legend("topright", label, bty = "n", cex = 3)
  if(add_mean == TRUE){
    mtext("E(X)", side = 1, at = sum(x * p), col = "red", line = 2)
  }
}

discrete_cdf <- function(x, p, xlim = c(min(x) - 1, max(x) + 1), label = ""){
  closeddot = cumsum(p)
  opencircle = c(0, closeddot[1:length(x)-1])
  plot(x, closeddot, pch = 19, cex = 1,
       ylim = c(0, 1),
       ylab = "", main = "", xlab = "",
       yaxt = "n",
       xlim = xlim,
       xaxt = "n",
       #yaxs = "i", 
       bty = "n")
  points(x, opencircle, cex = 1)
  segments(c(xlim[1], x), c(0, closeddot), c(x, xlim[2]), c(0, closeddot), lwd = 1)
  axis(1, at = floor(xlim[1]):ceiling(xlim[2]), cex.axis = 1)
  axis(2, at = seq(0, 1, length.out = 11), las = 1, cex.axis = 1.5)
  legend("bottomright", label, bty = "n", cex = 3)
}

# Define UI for application that draws a histogram
ui <- fluidPage(
  
  # Application title
  titlePanel("Binomial distribution PMF"),
  
  # Sidebar with a slider input for number of bins 
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("p",
                  "Probability of success (p):",
                  min = 0,
                  max = 1,
                  value = 0.5,
                  step = 0.01),
      sliderInput("n",
                  "Number of trials (n):",
                  min = 1,
                  max = 100,
                  value = 5,
                  step = 1)
    ),
    
    # Show a plot of the generated distribution
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("distPlot")
    )
  )
)

# Define server logic required to draw a histogram
server <- function(input, output) {
  
  output$distPlot <- renderPlot({
    
    p <- input$p
    n <- input$n

    #par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 2))
    
    #discrete_cdf(0:n, dbinom(0:n, n, p))
    discrete_pmf(0:n, dbinom(0:n, n, p), add_mean = TRUE)
    
  })
}

# Run the application 
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

## The standard normal and its CDF {.scrollable}

The special case $Z\sim\text{N}(0,1)$ is the **standard normal**.

Its CDF is traditionally denoted by $\Phi$:

$$
\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)=\int_{-\infty}^{z}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-t^2/2}\,dt.
$$

Unlike the uniform or exponential CDF, this integral **cannot be expressed using elementary functions**. But computers evaluate it to high precision.

```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 600)
plot(x, pnorm(x), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue4",
     xlab = "z", ylab = "Phi(z)", main = "The standard normal CDF")
abline(h = c(0, 0.5, 1), lty = 3, col = "grey65")
abline(v = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey65")
```

## Probabilities are areas, not heights {.scrollable}

For $X\sim\text{N}(70, 10^2)$, picture $P(60<X<85)$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(30, 110, length.out = 900)
y <- dnorm(x, 70, 10)
plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue4",
     xlab = "Value", ylab = "Density", main = "P(60 < X < 85)")
inside <- x >= 60 & x <= 85
polygon(c(60, x[inside], 85), c(0, y[inside], 0),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.45), border = NA)
lines(x, y, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue4")
abline(v = c(60, 85), lty = 3)
```

$$P(60<X<85)=F(85)-F(60).$$

Because $X$ is continuous, $P(X=60)=0$: including or excluding endpoints makes no difference.

## R's familiar `pdqr` family {.scrollable}

| Task | Normal distribution |
|---|---|
| PDF height at $x$ | `dnorm(x, mean, sd)` |
| CDF $P(X\le x)$ | `pnorm(x, mean, sd)` |
| Quantile (probability $p$) | `qnorm(p, mean, sd)` |
| Generate $n$ observations | `rnorm(n, mean, sd)` |

**R takes the standard deviation**, not the variance.

```{r}
dnorm(70, mean = 70, sd = 10)
pnorm(85, mean = 70, sd = 10) - pnorm(60, mean = 70, sd = 10)
qnorm(0.95, mean = 70, sd = 10)
```

## A warm-up: the class's new grading machine {.scrollable}

A malfunctioning grading machine produces scores that are approximately normal, with mean 75 and standard deviation 12. (For the purpose of this exercise, pretend scores can exceed 100.)

Let $X\sim\text{N}(75,12^2)$.

Compute in R:

1. $P(X<60)$: a decidedly unhappy student.
2. $P(X\ge90)$: a very happy student.
3. $P(70<X<85)$: comfortably in the middle.
4. The score at the **90th percentile**.

Try these before looking at the next slide.

## Grading machine: solutions {.scrollable}

```{r}
pnorm(60, mean = 75, sd = 12)

pnorm(90, mean = 75, sd = 12, lower.tail = FALSE)

pnorm(85, mean = 75, sd = 12) -
  pnorm(70, mean = 75, sd = 12)

qnorm(0.9, mean = 75, sd = 12)
```

**Question:** How could the machine produce scores over 100? Is a normal model always sensible for bounded quantities?

## Your turn: airport security's suspiciously precise clock {.scrollable}

According to an airline's optimistic brochure, the time $T$ (minutes) spent in a security line follows

$$T\sim\text{N}(24,6^2).$$

1. What is the probability of clearing security in **under 15 minutes**?
2. What is the probability of waiting **between 20 and 30 minutes**?
3. The airline claims that **95% of passengers wait less than $t$ minutes**. Find $t$.
4. Generate 10,000 hypothetical waiting times and approximate the answer to (1) by simulation.
5. How many simulated waiting times are negative? What does that tell you about this model?

*The distribution is chosen for computing practice, not because airport queues really are Gaussian.*

## Airport: a visual hint {.scrollable}

```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(0, 50, length.out = 800)
y <- dnorm(x, 24, 6)
plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue4",
     xlab = "Minutes", ylab = "Density", main = "Less than 15 minutes")
i <- x <= 15
polygon(c(0, x[i], 15), c(0, y[i], 0),
        col = adjustcolor("tomato3", alpha.f = 0.5), border = NA)
lines(x, y, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue4")
abline(v = 15, lty = 2)
```

## Airport: solutions {.scrollable}

```{r}
pnorm(15, mean = 24, sd = 6)

pnorm(30, mean = 24, sd = 6) -
  pnorm(20, mean = 24, sd = 6)

qnorm(0.95, mean = 24, sd = 6)

set.seed(240)
times <- rnorm(10000, mean = 24, sd = 6)
mean(times < 15)
sum(times < 0)
```

# Part 2: The gamma distribution

## First, remember the exponential {.scrollable}

The exponential distribution models positive quantities, often **waiting times**.

$$X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\beta),\qquad f_X(x)=\beta e^{-\beta x},\quad x>0.$$

- $\beta>0$ is the **rate**.
- $E(X)=1/\beta$.
- Its density decreases from its maximum at zero.

```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(0, 8, length.out = 600)
plot(x, dexp(x, rate = 1), type = "l", col = "steelblue4", lwd = 3,
     xlab = "Waiting time", ylab = "Density", main = "Exponential(rate = 1)")
```

The gamma family will give us many more shapes, while retaining positive support.

## Meet the gamma {.scrollable}

For $\alpha>0$ and $\beta>0$, a random variable has the gamma distribution if

$$
f_X(x)=\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x},\qquad x>0,
$$

and $f_X(x)=0$ for $x<0$.

We write $X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)$.

- $\alpha$: **shape** parameter.
- $\beta$: **rate** parameter.
- $E(X)=\alpha/\beta$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\alpha/\beta^2$ (derivations later).

**Important:** Some books use a *scale* parameter instead. Our $\beta$ is a **rate**.

## Gamma PDF = constant $\times$ kernel {.scrollable}

Here is the same structure again:

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}}_{\text{normalizing constant}}
\;\times\;
\underbrace{x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x}}_{\text{kernel (unnormalized density)}},
\qquad x>0.
$$

- For fixed $\alpha$ and $\beta$, only the **kernel** depends on $x$.
- The factor involving $\Gamma(\alpha)$ ensures that the total area is 1.
- This is the same organizational trick we've used for other PMFs and PDFs. **Spot the constant; spot the kernel.**

```{r}
#| echo: false
alpha <- 3; beta <- 1
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 700)
kernel <- x^(alpha - 1) * exp(-beta * x)
plot(x, kernel, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#D55E00",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Height",
     main = "Gamma(shape = 3, rate = 1): kernel versus PDF")
lines(x, dgamma(x, shape = alpha, rate = beta),
      lwd = 3, col = "#0072B2")
legend("topright", c("Kernel", "Normalized PDF"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
```

## What's that capital gamma? {.scrollable}

The gamma function is

$$\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,dt,\qquad a>0.$$

For positive integers, $\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!$.

```{r}
gamma(1)
gamma(4)
factorial(3)
gamma(2.5)
```

It supplies the normalizing constant that makes the gamma PDF integrate to 1. We will study the mathematical details elsewhere.

## Exponential is gamma in disguise {.scrollable}

When $\alpha=1$, since $\Gamma(1)=1$,

$$\frac{\beta^1}{\Gamma(1)}x^{1-1}e^{-\beta x}=\beta e^{-\beta x}.$$

So **$\operatorname{Gamma}(1,\beta)=\operatorname{Exp}(\beta)$**.

```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(0, 7, length.out = 600)
plot(x, dexp(x, rate = 1), type = "l", col = "#D55E00", lwd = 4,
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Density", main = "Two names, the same distribution")
lines(x, dgamma(x, shape = 1, rate = 1), col = "#0072B2", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Exponential(1)", "Gamma(shape=1, rate=1)"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2"), lwd = c(4, 2), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

## How do the parameters control the shape? {.small .scrollable}

- Keep the rate $\beta=1$ fixed and change shape;
- Keep the shape $\alpha=3$ fixed and change rate.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 500

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Gamma distribution DF"),
  
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("alpha", "Shape (α):",
                  min = 0.5, max = 20, value = 2, step = 0.1),
      sliderInput("beta", "Rate (β):",
                  min = 0.2, max = 10, value = 0.5, step = 0.05),
      hr(),
      verbatimTextOutput("moments")
    ),
    
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("gammaPlot", height = "600px")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$moments <- renderText({
    alpha <- input$alpha
    beta  <- input$beta
    mu <- alpha / beta
    sd <- sqrt(alpha) / beta
    paste0("E(X) = ", round(mu, 3),
           "\nsd(X) = ", round(sd, 3))
  })
  
  output$gammaPlot <- renderPlot({
    alpha <- input$alpha
    beta  <- input$beta
    
    # Fixed plotting range
    x_min <- -2
    x_max <- 25
    x <- seq(x_min, x_max, length.out = 2000)
    
    # PDF and CDF
    pdf_vals <- ifelse(x >= 0, dgamma(x, shape = alpha, rate = beta), 0)
    cdf_vals <- ifelse(x >= 0, pgamma(x, shape = alpha, rate = beta), 0)
    
    mu <- alpha / beta
    
    # Fixed y-limits
    pdf_ylim <- c(0, 0.8)
    cdf_ylim <- c(0, 1)
    

    
    # --- PDF ---
    plot(x, pdf_vals, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "darkred",
         xlim = c(x_min, x_max), ylim = pdf_ylim,
         main = "Probability Density Function (PDF)",
         xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)")
    #abline(v = mu, col = "gray60", lty = 3)
    
    # Label E(X) with mtext along x-axis
    if (mu >= x_min && mu <= x_max) {
      mtext("E(X)",
            side = 1, line = 2.2, at = mu, cex = 1.0)
    }
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)


```

## A gamma from familiar exponential variables {.scrollable}

Suppose $W_1,W_2,\ldots,W_k$ are **independent** exponential random variables, all with rate $\beta$.

Then their sum has a gamma distribution:

$$
W_1+\cdots+W_k\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(k,\beta).
$$

- One exponential waiting time is $\operatorname{Gamma}(1,\beta)$.
- The total of three independent exponential waiting times is $\operatorname{Gamma}(3,\beta)$.
- This gives us a concrete interpretation when the shape $k$ is a positive integer. **No proof needed today.**

```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(0, 12, length.out = 600)
plot(x, dgamma(x, 1, rate = 0.7), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#D55E00",
     ylim = c(0, 0.72), xlab = "Total waiting time", ylab = "Density",
     main = "Sum of 1, 3, or 5 independent exponential waits")
lines(x, dgamma(x, 3, rate = 0.7), lwd = 3, col = "#0072B2")
lines(x, dgamma(x, 5, rate = 0.7), lwd = 3, col = "#009E73")
legend("topright", c("1 wait", "3 waits", "5 waits"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#009E73"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
```

## R's gamma commands {.scrollable}

| Task | Gamma distribution |
|---|---|
| PDF height | `dgamma(x, shape, rate)` |
| CDF | `pgamma(x, shape, rate)` |
| Quantile | `qgamma(p, shape, rate)` |
| Simulation | `rgamma(n, shape, rate)` |

```{r}
dgamma(2, shape = 3, rate = 1)
pgamma(2, shape = 3, rate = 1)
qgamma(0.9, shape = 3, rate = 1)
rgamma(5, shape = 3, rate = 1)
```

**Warning:** `scale = 1 / rate`. We will use `rate =` explicitly throughout.

## The campus coffee emergency {.scrollable}

A terrifyingly elaborate coffee machine makes your latte in **four successive stages**: grinding, brewing, steaming, and "artisanal finishing." Each stage takes an independent $\operatorname{Exp}(0.5)$ number of minutes.

Let $T$ be the **total** time. Then

$$T=W_1+W_2+W_3+W_4\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(4,0.5).$$

Why is the rate **0.5**, rather than 2, when each stage takes 2 minutes *on average*?

Compute:

1. $P(T<5)$: the student might reach lecture on time.
2. $P(T>12)$: time to reconsider one's life choices.
3. $P(4<T<10)$.
4. The 90th percentile of $T$.

## Coffee emergency: picture {.scrollable}

```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(0, 22, length.out = 900)
y <- dgamma(x, shape = 4, rate = 0.5)
plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue4",
     xlab = "Minutes", ylab = "Density", main = "Time until the fourth order")
i <- x <= 5
polygon(c(0, x[i], 5), c(0, y[i], 0),
        col = adjustcolor("tomato3", alpha.f = 0.5), border = NA)
lines(x, y, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue4")
abline(v = 5, lty = 2)
```

## Coffee emergency: solutions {.scrollable}

```{r}
pgamma(5, shape = 4, rate = 0.5)

pgamma(12, shape = 4, rate = 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE)

pgamma(10, shape = 4, rate = 0.5) -
  pgamma(4, shape = 4, rate = 0.5)

qgamma(0.9, shape = 4, rate = 0.5)
```

## Your turn: haunted house jump scares {.scrollable}

A haunted house contains **five rooms**, each with an independent, exponentially distributed amount of time before a jump scare. In each room, the waiting time has rate **3 per hour**. (Management refuses refunds.)

Let $T$ be the **total waiting time across all five rooms**, measured in hours.

1. Identify the distribution of $T$, including its parameters.
2. Find $P(T<1)$.
3. Find $P(T>2)$.
4. Find the smallest $t$ such that $P(T\le t)=0.75$.
5. Generate 10,000 observations of $T$ and estimate $P(T>2)$ using simulation.

## One last picture: simulation versus theory {.scrollable}

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(240)
t <- rgamma(10000, shape = 5, rate = 3)
hist(t, breaks = 50, probability = TRUE, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     xlab = "Total waiting time across five rooms", main = "10,000 simulated haunted-house visits")
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 5, rate = 3), add = TRUE,
      col = "#D55E00", lwd = 3)
legend("topright", "Gamma(5, rate = 3) PDF", col = "#D55E00", lwd = 3, bty = "n")
```

The histogram approximates a density, not a PMF. Why is `probability = TRUE` necessary here?

## Haunted house: solutions {.scrollable}

$T\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(5,3)$.

```{r}
pgamma(1, shape = 5, rate = 3)

pgamma(2, shape = 5, rate = 3, lower.tail = FALSE)

qgamma(0.75, shape = 5, rate = 3)

set.seed(240)
t <- rgamma(10000, shape = 5, rate = 3)
mean(t > 2)
```
